title: Goodness-of-fit
subtitle: We're all just high-dimensional data
html:
Can we talk about statistics for a second 😅?

In statistics, goodness-of-fit is an assessment of how well a model’s expectations align with observed data. This means that goodness-of-fit depends on two things: expectations and observations.

Consider the Chi-square statistic—a goodness-of-fit measurement—where Oi is the observed data, and Ei is the expected:

χ2=∑i(Oi−Ei)2Ei\chi^2 = \sum_{i}\frac{(O_{i} - E_{i})^2}{E_i}

The part of the equation that does the heavy lifting is (Oi — Ei)2. It’s the difference between observations (Oi) and the expectations (Ei) (squared). Large differences between these two values create a large Chi-square value, demonstrating a statistically significant difference between the observations and the expectations1. Put simply, more different == worse fit.

But what if we think of the data as people, and we’re observing ourselves against the backdrop of our environment? If we’re the observations, what are the expectations?

The expectations are the culture and customs of the people you engage with: the way they act, the way they interact, and what they deem to be the generally-recognized-as-safe levels of friendliness, intelligence, and ambition. I say generally-recognized-as-safe because all these facets—the culture, the customs, etc.—define the set of parameters within which you must exist to feel like you belong. When you deviate too far from their mean values—when you cease to be average—you no longer fit in.

If we are living well, meaning we are growing and adapting, then we’re likely to experience many instances in which we no longer fit in with the people we once considered “our people”. When our personal Chi-square statistic increases to the point where we’re significantly different than our peers, we’re faced with a choice: we either keep carving a path in the world that is uniquely ours and find a new environment with new expectations, or we can squander our potential to maintain relationships with people who don’t want what we want and don’t see the world how we see it.

If we stay where we are and pretend to be someone we’re not, we give up discovery to cling to familiarity, even when familiarity itself is not comfortable. We remain located in region-beta2—in enough pain to hurt, but not enough pain to leave.

If, however, we choose to go our own way, there will be more pain in the near-term than if we stayed in region-beta surrounded by people who don’t quite get us. There will be an uncomfortable middle when we’re too dissimilar to the people we used to hang out with for them to accept us, but not similar enough to the people we want to hang out with to be accepted by them. This is the lonely chapter. And it’ll take time to surround ourselves with people like us—people for whom our Chi-square statistic is small, people with whom we fit.

And that’s okay.

Becoming an outlier is dramatically less scary when you realize that we can just find a new distribution.

P.S.

The more I write, the more I realize that I’m not saying anything new. I’m mostly just packaging and repackaging cliches in ways that make sense to me. And that’s fine! It may feel like overcomplicating, but, in my opinion, sometimes (usually) it takes drowning in complexity before you’re able to recognize what’s essential.

1

A slight oversimplification, but we’ll leave degrees of freedom out of the discussion.

2

The region-beta paradox describes the phenomenon in which people will “recover more quickly from more distressing experiences than from less distressing ones.” Similar to the idea of golden handcuffs: painful, but not so painful that you leave.
